meta.blurb: Mira is twenty-eight, has some savings and a card bill, and has never bought a share. Her cousin Dev, who once sold in a panic and regretted it, shows her what shares, bonds and index funds are, and why costs matter.
meta.bible:
Mira: a careful young woman of twenty-eight who has never invested; she starts with two hundred dollars a month and keeps going. Dev: her cousin, a bookkeeper who has invested quietly for ten years; patient and honest; he once sold in a panic and regretted it. Money is counted in dollars. Mira pays off a card debt of six hundred dollars before she invests. In the fourteenth month the market falls by roughly a fifth; Mira reads her written plan and keeps investing. Five years later she has paid in twelve thousand dollars and her account is worth a little more. Illustrations, never forecasts: ten thousand dollars growing at six percent a year for thirty years becomes about fifty-seven thousand dollars, and at five percent about forty-three thousand; two hundred dollars a month for thirty years at an average of six percent a year becomes about two hundred thousand dollars on seventy-two thousand paid in. Key terms: Share, Shares, Bond, Bonds, Fund, Index, Index fund, Expense ratio, Dividends, Diversification, Broker, Platform, Regulated, Adviser, Pension, Compounding, Inflation, Emergency fund, Speculating, Investing, Saving. Voice: calm, practical and kind; every fact is true and hedged; no real brands, funds or people; general information and not personal financial advice; tax and pension rules differ by country. More names and facts: Sana: a friendly colleague of Mira at a small printing company who later asks how to start. Tomas: a colleague who loves hot tips and fashionable coins. Bea: an old school friend who whispers a tip at a restaurant. Mr Hale: the owner of the printing company. Ms Lindqvist: a fee-only adviser Mira meets once. Anita: Dev's wife. Rohan: their young son. Dev keeps a worn notebook with his own rules, and Mira keeps a plain notebook with her written plan: keep investing every month, do not sell in a fall, review once a year. Terms: Stock market, Exchange, Coupon, Maturity, Yield, Rebalancing, Volatility, Drawdown, Spread, Ticker, Tracker, Allocation, Horizon, Pension, ETF, Fee, Inflation.
In the fall Mira's account, which holds mostly shares and some bonds, falls by a little less than the market; she adds a fourth rule to her notebook: wait three days before any decision.

B1B2: Mira is twenty-eight, and for three years she has saved a little each month. She wonders whether there is a better place for her money than an ordinary bank account.
Last year her savings earned only a few dollars of interest, and Mira circles the line in pencil. It feels a little like watching a plant that never seems to grow.
Dev works as a bookkeeper, and he has been investing for ten years without ever mentioning it at family dinners. Mira rings him, and he laughs and invites her to come on Sunday.
Dev tells Mira at the start that he will not tell her what to buy. He only wants her to understand how it works, so that she can decide for herself.
The flat line shows her bank money, and the rising line shows prices in the shops. Dev explains that prices usually go up over time, even if the number in your account stays the same.

Suppose that prices rise by two percent each year, which is common in many countries. Then a basket of shopping that costs one hundred dollars today would cost about one hundred and twenty-two dollars in ten years.
Dev says this is called inflation, and it makes cash lose buying power. If the bank pays less than prices rise, your money buys a little less each year, even though the number does not fall.
Mira admits that investing frightens her, because she has read stories about people who lost everything or were tricked. Dev says that the fear is sensible and that it is a good place to start.
Dev tells her that no honest person can promise a return, and that anyone who offers quick riches is usually selling something. Real investing, he says, is slow, plain and a little boring.
Dev hands Mira a notebook and tells her to write down every question and, later, every decision. On the first page she writes one line: what is my money for?
Dev puts a packet of seeds, a bag of coins and a casino chip on the table. He says that people often mix up saving, investing and speculating, but that they are three different things.
Saving means keeping your money safe and easy to reach, so that you can spend it when you need it. It will not grow fast, but it will not suddenly fall either.
Investing means putting money into things that may grow or pay you an income, such as companies. The value can fall as well as rise, so you need years of patience.

Speculating means betting that a price will change quickly, and it is closer to a casino than to a garden. Studies in several countries suggest that people who trade very often tend to do worse than people who simply hold.
Dev explains that in investing, a higher possible reward comes with bigger ups and downs. If someone offers high returns with no risk, he says, they are either mistaken or not honest.
Dev explains that your time horizon is how long you can leave the money alone. A common rule of thumb is that money you will need within about five years should not be in shares.
Dev says that over very long periods, shares in many countries have grown more than cash, but with some deep falls along the way. He adds that the past is not a promise about the future.
Dev suggests that Mira thinks of three jars, labelled now, soon and later. The first holds money for bills, the second holds savings for the next few years, and only the third is for investing.
Dev asks a hard question: how would you feel if your account fell by a fifth in a few weeks? He tells her to answer honestly, because many people discover the answer only when it happens.
In her notebook Mira writes her first rule: only money I will not need for at least ten years goes into investing. Dev says that it is a very good rule to begin with.
Dev says that investing has an order, and the first steps are not exciting. He writes a short checklist: an emergency fund, no expensive debt, a clear goal and a written plan.
An emergency fund is money kept aside for sudden problems, such as a broken tooth or a lost job. If you have one, you will not have to sell your investments at a bad time.

Mira sits with a calculator and adds up what she must pay each month: rent, food, transport and her phone. The total is smaller than she feared, and she is surprised that she has never worked it out before.

Dividing her savings by her monthly costs, Mira finds that she could live for about five months without any pay. Dev says that those savings are her emergency fund, and that she should not invest them.
Mira confesses that she owes six hundred dollars on her credit card. Dev asks what the interest rate is, and she finds that it is more than twenty percent a year.
Dev says that paying off a debt with twenty percent interest is like earning twenty percent with no risk. No honest investment can promise anything like that, so the card must come first.

That same month, Mira pays the six hundred dollars from her savings and watches the balance turn to zero. She still has about four months of costs saved, and she feels lighter than she has for a long time.
Dev asks whether Mira has basic insurance for the things that would be very costly to lose. In many countries, insurance protects against large bills, so it is worth checking what you already have.
On an index card, Mira writes down two goals for her money. One is feeling secure in later life, about thirty years away, and the other is saving for a home, perhaps within seven years.
At last every box on the checklist is ticked. Dev says that the order matters as much as the choices, and that Mira is now ready to learn what to invest in.
Dev imagines a busy bakery that needs a bigger oven but does not have the money. So the owner sells small slices of the business to many people, and each slice is called a share.
Suppose the bakery has a thousand shares, and you buy ten of them. You then own one percent of the bakery, and one percent of everything it earns.
People who own shares can earn money in two quite different ways. The price of the share may rise, and the company may pay a part of its profit to its owners, which is called a dividend.

A stock exchange is a market where shares are bought and sold, and today most of the trading is done by computer. The price of a share changes all day, because it depends on what buyers and sellers will agree to pay.
A share price moves when people change their view of the company's future profits. In the short term it is full of noise, but over many years it tends to follow how much the business really earns.
Dev reminds her that a company can fail, perhaps because of a rival or a bad idea or bad luck. If it closes, its shareholders are paid after everyone else, so they can lose all of their money.
Large, well-known companies are usually steadier, because they have many customers and a lot of experience. Small companies can grow faster, but they can also fall further, and more of them fail.
Dev says that owning shares means owning part of real businesses that make things, sell things and employ people. The growth in the long run comes from their work, and not from any trick.

Walking home, Mira notices how many things in her life belong to companies: her phone, her bus, her supermarket. She realises that she is already a customer of many businesses that she could also own.
Dev repeats the most important point about shares: they offer a chance of growth, but never a promise of it. Mira writes in her notebook: a share is a slice of a business, and it is not a guarantee.
Next Dev explains the second building block, which is the bond. With a share you become an owner, but with a bond you become a lender, and the borrower promises to pay you back with interest.
Dev gives an example with made-up numbers: you lend one thousand dollars for ten years at four percent. Every year you receive forty dollars, and at the end you get the thousand back.
Governments sell bonds to pay for things such as roads and schools. Companies do the same to build new factories or to grow, and so the bond market is huge.
A borrower might fail to pay back what it owes, which is called credit risk. A risky borrower has to offer a higher rate of interest to attract lenders, so a very high rate is often a warning.
You can sell a bond before it ends, but its price changes. If interest rates rise, new bonds pay more than old ones, so older bonds become less attractive and their price falls.
Dev says that bonds usually move up and down less than shares, but they are not safe. They can lose value, and if prices rise fast, their fixed payments buy less and less.

In a collection of investments, bonds can add a steady income and a cushion when shares fall. The price for that comfort is that, over very long periods, they have usually grown more slowly than shares.

Dev draws a ladder of three steps, with cash at the bottom because it is the safest and slowest. Bonds are in the middle, and shares are at the top, with the highest chance of growth and the biggest swings.
Mira asks which is better, shares or bonds, but Dev says that it is not a contest. They do different jobs, and most people own both through funds that hold many bonds or shares at once.
In her notebook Mira draws two columns, one for the owner and one for the lender. The owner shares in profit and loss, while the lender is paid first but receives only the amount that was promised.
Dev warns that putting all your money into one company is a very risky plan. Even excellent businesses can fail, and no one can reliably tell in advance which ones will.
A fund collects money from many people and uses it to buy hundreds or even thousands of shares at once. Each person owns a small part of the whole basket, called units.

Spreading money across many different investments, instead of a few, is called diversification. Because companies do not all fall at the same time, it lowers the risk without lowering the hoped-for return very much.
Mira tries a small experiment on paper, using three companies that she likes. She writes down their prices, and after a month she finds that one has risen, one has fallen and one has hardly moved.
Dev says that even professionals cannot reliably choose which companies will do best. The winners of one year are often not the winners of the next, so chasing them is a poor plan.
Each unit of a fund has a price, which is shown on the website every day. When the shares inside the basket rise or fall, the unit price moves by about the same amount.

There are two common kinds of fund: ordinary funds, priced once a day, and exchange-traded funds, which are bought and sold all day like shares. Dev says that cost and contents matter more than the label.
Dev warns that not every fund is truly spread out. Some hold only one industry or one small country, which brings back the same risk, so you should always check what is inside.
