He wrote a short checklist headed before you invest: an emergency fund, no expensive debt, a clear goal and a written plan. Most beginners skip straight to the last part of the process, he said, and that is exactly why so many of them come to regret it.

An emergency fund, Dev explained, is money set aside for the sudden problems that arrive without warning, such as a broken tooth, a car repair or the loss of a job. Its purpose is to protect your investments rather than to earn anything itself, because without it a bad month could force you to sell at exactly the wrong moment. A common rule of thumb is to hold three to six months of essential costs, kept somewhere safe and easy to reach.

Mira sat down with her calculator and added up what she had to pay every month, leaving out everything optional: the rent, the food, the bus pass, the phone and the small bills that hid in the corners. The total was a little smaller than she had feared, and she was startled to realise that she had never actually worked it out in all her years of earning. Knowing the exact number, she felt, was already a kind of quiet strength, and it made the whole subject less foggy.

When she divided her savings by her monthly costs, Mira discovered that she could live for about five months even if her pay stopped altogether. Dev told her that this money was therefore her emergency fund, and that it should stay exactly where it was, safe and boring and available. It was the first time she had understood that her savings were not a failure to invest but a foundation to build upon.

With a small blush, Mira confessed that she still owed six hundred dollars on her credit card, left over from a winter of unplanned spending. Dev asked what interest the card charged, and when she checked the paperwork she found that it was more than twenty percent a year, which made her wince. The balance had been sitting there quietly, growing like a weed in a flower bed.

Dev put it in a way that she never forgot: clearing a debt that charges more than twenty percent a year is the same as earning a guaranteed twenty percent, with no risk and no waiting. No honest investment could ever promise anything of the kind, and so, however tempting the stock market might seem, the card had to come first. The most reliable return, he said, is often the debt you no longer owe.

That very month Mira paid the six hundred dollars from her savings, pressing the button and watching the balance on her screen turn to zero. She still had about four months of costs set aside, which was more than enough for a cushion, and she felt a weight lift from her shoulders that she had not noticed she was carrying. It was not an investment in the usual sense, but it was the best one she had made so far.

Dev also asked whether Mira had basic insurance for the few things that would be ruinous to lose or replace, such as her health cover, her belongings and, if she had one, her bicycle. In many countries such cover protects against bills that no ordinary savings could absorb, and he thought it wise to see what she already had before adding anything new. She made a note to read her policies properly, which she had never done before.

On an index card, Mira wrote down her goals and, beside each of them, the number of years she would need to wait. The first was lasting security in later life, about thirty years away, and the second was a modest home of her own, perhaps within seven years. Dev observed that the two ambitions demanded different kinds of money, and that only the former suited investing.

At last every box on the checklist had a tick beside it, and Mira stared at the page with a small private pride. Dev said that the order of these steps matters at least as much as the choices that follow them, and that most of the trouble in the world of money comes from people doing them backwards. Now, and only now, he said, they could talk about what one actually buys.

Dev began with a story about an imaginary bakery on a busy street, where the queue reached the pavement every morning and the single oven could not keep pace. The owner needed money for a bigger one, and instead of borrowing it she sold small slices of the business to many different people, each slice being called a share. Everyone who bought a slice became, in a small way, a part-owner of the bakery.

Dev made the arithmetic simple by supposing that the bakery had a thousand shares in all, of which Mira bought ten. She would then own exactly one percent of the business, with a claim on one percent of whatever it earned and kept. It was a tiny share of a small shop, he said, but the same principle applied to the largest companies in the world, whose ownership is divided into billions of slices.

A shareholder, Dev explained, can gain in two quite separate ways, and it helps to keep them apart in the mind. The price of the share may rise as the business grows more valuable, and the company may also pay out a portion of its profit to its owners in regular payments known as dividends. Neither is guaranteed, he cautioned, because a company that earns nothing has nothing to give, and its share price is likely to reflect that.

The place where shares are traded, Dev said, is called a stock exchange, and although the old picture of shouting crowds survives in films, nearly all of the buying and selling is now done by computer. The price of a share is not fixed by anyone in charge but changes moment by moment, according to what buyers are willing to pay and sellers are willing to accept. Mira found this oddly comforting, because it meant that the price was simply an opinion that happened to be written in numbers.

Why do prices move, Mira wanted to know, and Dev answered that they move when people change their opinion about a company's likely future profits, and sometimes merely because their mood changes. In the short term the movements are mostly noise, which means that a good company can fall for no clear reason and a poor one can rise. Over many years, however, prices tend to follow what the businesses actually earn, and that was the idea he asked her to trust.

The story could end badly, Dev warned: a rival might open across the road, the ovens might break, or the baker might simply make poor decisions, and the bakery would have to close. When a company closes, its debts are paid first and its shareholders come last in the queue, which means that a share in a failed business can become worthless. That was the price of ownership, and he wanted her to know it before she paid anything at all.

Companies come in all sizes, Dev observed, and the size matters to the kind of ride one gets. Large, well-established firms tend to be steadier because they have many customers and long experience, whereas small and young ones can grow much faster but are also more likely to stumble or disappear. Neither type is better in every season, and together they form the full range of what a broad collection of shares contains.

When you own a share, Dev told her, you are not holding a lottery ticket but a small piece of a real business that makes things, sells things and gives work to people. The returns that investors have earned over the long run have come from that ordinary activity, from products invented, customers served and profits earned, and not from any clever trick. This, he said, was why shares deserved to be taken seriously, and why they also deserved to be treated with humility.

Walking home along the high street, Mira began to see the world differently, because she noticed how many of the things in her daily life were made, run or sold by companies. Her phone, her bus, her supermarket and even the coffee in her cup all belonged to businesses whose shares could be owned by anybody, including her. She was already a customer of the economy, and it struck her as strange that she had never thought of being a part-owner.

Before she left that evening, Dev repeated the one point that he wanted her to carry away: owning shares offers a chance of growth, but it never offers a promise of it. Mira wrote it in her notebook in her own words, a share is a slice of a business and not a guarantee, and he nodded as if she had passed an important test. Then they washed the cups together and talked about nothing in particular, which was also a pleasure.

The second building block, Dev said, is the bond, and it works in almost exactly the opposite way from a share. With a share you become a part-owner of a business, but with a bond you become a lender, and the borrower, which may be a company or a government, promises to pay you back with interest. Mira liked the neat symmetry of it, and wrote owner and lender on a fresh page.

Dev gave her a simple example with invented numbers: suppose you lend a thousand dollars for ten years at four percent. You would receive forty dollars every year, called the coupon, and on the final date, called maturity, your original thousand would come back. The arrangement was as plain as a rental agreement, he said, and that plainness was its charm.

Who wants to borrow all this money, Mira asked, and Dev replied that the answer is nearly everyone with a big project. Governments sell bonds to pay for roads, hospitals and schools, and companies do the same to build factories or expand into new markets, so the bond market is in fact enormous. Behind the quiet word bond there stand bridges, buses, breweries and a whole world of ordinary ambition that needs financing.

Every lender faces the danger that the borrower will be unable to pay, which is known as credit risk, and the markets price it carefully. A stable government will usually pay a modest rate because it is judged unlikely to default, while a shaky company must offer a much higher one to tempt anyone to lend at all. A very high interest rate, Dev warned, is therefore less often a bargain than a signal of trouble.

Bonds can be sold before their maturity date, Dev said, but their prices move, and the way they move surprised Mira at first. When interest rates rise, newly issued bonds pay more than old ones, so the old ones become less attractive and their prices fall, as if on a seesaw. A bond held to the end will still repay its full value if the borrower pays, but the journey can contain some bumps.

On the whole, Dev told her, bonds swing less wildly than shares, which is why many people find them calming, but they are by no means risk-free. Their price can fall when interest rates rise, the borrower can fail, and if inflation climbs quickly the fixed payments begin to buy less and less. Like everything else in his lessons, bonds had a purpose and a price, and the sensible course was to know both before buying.

Why own bonds at all, then, if shares tend to grow more over the long run? Dev explained that bonds can provide a steady income and a cushion when shares fall, and that the cushion is worth having even though it usually comes at the cost of slower growth over the decades. He compared them to the brakes of a car, which make it slower but also make it possible to drive it sensibly.

On the back of an envelope Dev drew a ladder of three steps and labelled them from the bottom up: cash, bonds and shares. As one climbed, the long-term growth that investors had enjoyed tended to be higher, but so were the ups and downs, and the ladder never offered one without the other. Mira copied it into her notebook, thinking that it was the most compact piece of knowledge she had ever been given.

Which is better, then, Mira asked after a pause, shares or bonds, and must a person really choose between them? Dev shook his head and said that the question was a little like asking whether a bicycle is better than a boat, because they do different jobs in different conditions. Most people, he added, own both, and the simplest way is through a fund that holds hundreds of bonds at once, which brings the same spreading of risk that she was about to meet with shares.

At the end of the evening Mira drew two columns in her notebook and headed them owner and lender, filling in each with what she had learned. The owner shares in the profit and the loss and may gain a great deal or lose it all, whereas the lender is paid first but receives only the fixed amount that was promised. Reading it back, she felt a rare pleasure at having made something confusing so clear that a child could follow it.

Dev warned her against the most tempting plan of all, which is to put all of one's money into a single company that seems to be doing well. Even excellent businesses can stumble, change with the times or simply be overtaken, and nobody has ever found a reliable way to tell in advance which ones will fail. History is crowded with famous names that once seemed permanent, and he did not want Mira to bet her future on one of them.

A fund, Dev explained, solves part of this problem by collecting money from a great many people and using it to buy the shares of hundreds or even thousands of companies at once. Each investor then owns a small portion of the whole basket, measured in units, and the failure of any single company has only a tiny effect on the total. It was a very old idea, he said, older than the stock markets themselves, and a thoroughly practical one.

This spreading of money across many investments is called diversification, and Dev called it the nearest thing to a free gift that investing has to offer. Because companies do not all stumble at once, a broad basket lowers the risk of a serious loss without necessarily lowering the return one can reasonably hope for. He added that it will not protect anyone from a general fall in markets, but it does protect against the single disaster.

Mira decided to test the idea with a small experiment that cost nothing, picking three companies she liked and writing their prices on a sheet of paper. A month later she looked again and found that one had risen, one had fallen and one had scarcely moved at all, with no connection that she could see to how good the products were. She learned more from that sheet than from an hour of reading, because she had seen for herself how much luck was involved.

Dev told her that even highly paid professionals have not been able to choose, year after year, which companies will do best, and that the winners of one year are frequently not the winners of the next. Chasing last year's stars is therefore a surprisingly poor strategy, because by the time the news reaches the public the surprise has usually been absorbed into the price. Mira thought of her three companies on their sheet of paper, one up and one down and one sleeping, and nodded, a little ruefully.

Each unit of a fund carries a price, Dev explained, and that price simply follows the total value of everything inside the basket, divided by the number of units. When the companies inside rise or fall, the unit price moves by roughly the same amount, less the small yearly fee that the fund charges. Mira found it reassuring that there was no mystery here, only a basket and a number that kept pace with it.

Funds come in two common wrappers, Dev told her: ordinary funds, which are priced once a day, and exchange-traded funds, often called ETFs, which are bought and sold throughout the day like shares. Either kind can hold the same things inside, and he said that the label mattered far less than two other questions, namely what was in the basket and what it cost. Mira wrote both questions at the top of a clean page, and underneath them she drew a small box for the answers.

Not every fund, Dev warned, is as broad as its cheerful name might suggest, because some hold only one industry, one theme or one small country. Such a fund brings back the very risk that diversification was meant to remove, since a bad year for that single corner of the market hurts all of it at once. The remedy was to open the fund's information sheet and read the list of what it actually owned.

Then Dev unrolled a long strip of paper and explained that an index is simply a list of companies, for instance the largest few hundred in a given country, chosen by clear and public rules. The bigger the company, the more it counts within the list, and the index number rises and falls with the total value of everything on it. An index is not something you can buy directly, he said, but it is something a fund can copy.

An index fund, Dev said at last, does not try to be clever: it simply copies an index by buying every company on the list in roughly the same proportions. Because it needs no team of expensive analysts hunting for winners, it can charge a very small fee, and that modest difference turns out to matter enormously over the years. Mira put down her pen and said that, put like that, it seemed almost too sensible to be true.

Dev described two ways of running a fund, the first of which he called active and the second passive. In the active way, a team of experts studies companies and tries to beat the market by choosing winners, whereas in the passive way, the index fund, nobody tries to win and the fund simply matches the average. It sounded to Mira as though the active way must be better, and she was a little surprised when Dev said that the evidence tells a different story.

Dev put the argument in a way that took only a few moments to follow. Before costs, all investors together own the whole market, so together they must earn the market's average return, and after the costs of all their research and trading have been taken away, the average must be lower. This simple sum, he said, is why studies in many countries have found that most active funds have trailed their index over long periods, though a few have not.

Mira showed Dev an advertisement for a list of top-performing funds, with stars and a handsome chart, and he asked her to consider who was missing from the picture. Funds that perform badly are often quietly closed or merged into others, so that only the survivors appear in the list, and the average of the survivors is naturally impressive. This effect, known as survivorship bias, makes the past of the whole industry look rosier than it really was.

Dev asked Mira to imagine a thousand people in a hall, each flipping a coin ten times, and pointed out that about one of them would be expected to throw ten heads in a row by pure chance. Nobody would call that person a genius, and yet in the world of funds a lucky streak of that kind is celebrated and advertised, and money flows towards it. Some managers are certainly skilled, Dev conceded, but telling skill from luck in advance is extraordinarily hard.

Then Dev showed her the sum that she would remember best of all, using illustrations and not forecasts. Ten thousand dollars growing at six percent a year for thirty years becomes about fifty-seven thousand dollars, whereas the same sum growing at five percent, after a fee of one percent, becomes only about forty-three thousand. That seemingly harmless percentage point, quietly repeated every year, would take around fourteen thousand dollars from her, and it would do so whether or not the market was kind.

The cruelty of fees, Dev pointed out, is that they are charged on the whole of your money every year, whatever the market has done, in good years and in bad. Returns are uncertain and fees are certain, which makes the fee the one part of the bargain that you can both see and choose in advance. A drop of water, he said, will wear down stone if it is allowed to fall long enough.

The yearly fee, Dev explained, is called the expense ratio, and by law in many countries it must appear on the fund's information sheet, usually under a heading such as ongoing charges. A fee of one tenth of one percent costs a dollar a year for every thousand dollars invested, whereas a fee of one percent costs ten dollars on the same thousand. Mira found the number on the sheet in front of her and circled it in pencil, feeling as if she had learned to read a new alphabet.

Mira laid out the information sheets of three broad funds side by side on the kitchen table, as she might compare three mobile phone plans. The lists of what they owned looked very much alike, which made sense, but the yearly fees were strikingly different, and the fee was the one clear difference she could find. Dev smiled, because in his experience that is almost always where the difference lies.

No investor, Dev told her, can control the market, the economy or the mood of the news, and spending energy on those is like shouting at the weather. What she could control was how much she paid, how widely she spread her money and how steadily she kept going, and of these three the cost was the easiest to fix on the very first day. He found that people who focused on what they could control tended to be calmer.

Dev added one honest warning, which was that an index fund is not magic and will fall whenever the market falls, and that low cost is no guarantee of a good result. Nevertheless, in many studies low-cost funds have tended to do better than expensive ones on average, and so Mira turned to a fresh page in her notebook and wrote a rule beneath the heading what I can control. It read, in her careful hand: choose a broad fund with a low yearly cost, and then leave it alone.

To buy a fund, Dev explained, one cannot simply walk into a shop and ask for a basket of companies. One needs an account with a broker or an investment platform, which is a company that acts as the middleman and lets you buy and sell investments through its website or its app. Choosing the right one, he added, is a decision worth making slowly, because a poor choice quietly costs money for years.

The first test, said Dev, is whether the platform is regulated, which means that a public authority has approved the company and can inspect and discipline it. In most countries the regulator keeps a public register, and a few minutes spent searching it for the firm's name is the cheapest protection a beginner can buy. He added that, in many places, a regulated platform must also keep customers' money apart from its own, though the rules differ.

Dev then gave a warning that he said was the most practical advice in the whole afternoon: criminals copy real websites, run polished advertisements and send friendly messages to strangers, all promising safe and guaranteed profits. He told Mira to type the address herself, to check the firm on the regulator's register, and to ignore anyone who contacted her first about an investment, however kind or convincing they seemed. A real platform, he said, never needs to hurry you, and anyone who rushes you is a reason to walk away.

Platforms earn their living in several ways, Dev told her, and the charges may include an account fee, a fee on every purchase, a fee for changing currencies and sometimes a penalty for being inactive. The prices are often buried several clicks down the page, and reading every line, though tedious, is the only way to find out what a platform will really cost. Mira opened a spreadsheet and began to fill in the numbers, line by patient line.

Mira noticed a trap on one of the three sites: a fixed charge of five dollars for every purchase. On a purchase of two hundred dollars that fee amounted to two and a half percent, taken immediately and every single month, which was far more than the entire yearly fee of a good index fund. The lesson, she saw, was that the best platform for a millionaire might be the worst one for a person who invests small amounts regularly.

After an evening of comparison, Mira chose a platform that was regulated, that stated its charges plainly and that did not penalise small monthly purchases. It also offered a simple way to invest a set amount automatically, and its website was clear enough that she could follow every step without calling for help. Dev looked over her list and said that she had done precisely what a careful person should do, and that it was not glamorous at all.

Dev mentioned that some countries offer special accounts in which the growth of an investment is taxed lightly, or not at all, usually within a yearly limit. The rules, the names and the limits differ greatly from one country to another, and they change from time to time, so he could not tell her what applied in her own case. He urged her to read the official guidance, or to ask a qualified tax adviser, before she opened anything.

A pension account, Dev continued, often comes with tax advantages, but the money is usually locked until a certain age, which can be a blessing for a person who might otherwise be tempted to spend it. Mira weighed the trade, since her long-term goal fitted the pension idea well but her home deposit would need to stay within reach. She decided to learn the rules properly and to use the tax-friendly route for her later-life money, if she could.

To open an account the platform needed to confirm who she was, so Mira gathered her passport, a recent utility bill showing her address, her bank details and her tax number. These checks are required by law in many countries in order to prevent fraud and money laundering, and the platform's website explained this briefly and politely. She photographed each document in good light and felt, for the first time, that investing was becoming real.

Mira sat at the kitchen table and filled in the form line by line, giving her name, her address and the details of the bank account that would feed her investments. The platform also asked a few questions about her experience and her attitude to risk, and she answered them honestly instead of trying to sound more daring than she was. When she pressed the button to send it, her heart beat a little faster, as if she were mailing a letter to her future self.

A few days later an email arrived to say that Mira's account had been approved, and she logged in to find a tidy page with a balance of zero. She sent two hundred dollars from her bank, which would take a day or two to appear, and she refreshed the screen several times with the impatience of a child waiting for a kettle to boil. The sum was small, but it felt like the opening of a door, and she meant to walk through it with care.

Mira asked Dev whether this was a good moment to begin, because the newspapers kept saying that prices looked high and the outlook looked uncertain. Dev laughed kindly and replied that prices always look too high or too frightening to somebody, and that in all his years he had never met a person who could name the perfect day in advance. Waiting for certainty, he said, is a plan that never actually starts, because certainty is never on offer.

Mira worked through her budget with a pencil and found that, after all her bills and a modest allowance for pleasure, she could comfortably invest two hundred dollars a month. It did not sound like much, and she said so, but Dev replied that the habit mattered far more than the amount. A person who keeps going for decades will usually beat one who starts big and then stops, he said, and Mira felt relieved that the entrance fee was not a fortune.

You do not need a large sum to start, Dev reminded her, any more than a gardener needs a large seed to grow a tall tree. A small beginning teaches the habits of patience and routine at a moment when mistakes are cheap, and the amount can always be raised later as pay grows and confidence rises. What cannot be recovered, he added, is the time that passes while one is waiting to feel ready.

Dev proposed a rule so simple that Mira nearly dismissed it: invest the same amount on the same day every month and keep going. It removes the need to guess about the market, it turns investing into a routine like paying the rent, and it means that no single month's news can decide anything important. The charm of the idea, he said, lay in how little it asked of her mind.

To show why a steady amount works so well, Dev used invented numbers: at twenty dollars a unit, two hundred dollars buys ten of them, but at ten dollars it buys twenty. Over the years a regular investor therefore buys more units when prices are low and fewer when they are high, which quietly improves the average price paid. It was not a trick for making profit from nothing, he added, only a sensible way of living with uncertainty.

Dev was honest enough to mention the other side of the argument: a person who receives a large sum may do better, on average, by investing it all at once. Markets have risen more often than they have fallen, but Mira was paid monthly and would invest monthly, and spreading a large sum over several months can calm a nervous person. Both approaches are reasonable, he said, and the best one is the one that you will actually follow.

Mira set up an automatic payment from her bank to leave on the day after her pay arrived, so that the investment would happen before she had a chance to spend the money on something else. Because she no longer had to make a decision each month, there was far less chance that she would skip a payment out of laziness or be talked out of it by a worrying headline. It was, she realised, the cheapest and most effective piece of self-discipline she had ever bought.

Dev gave her a short checklist for choosing the fund itself, and he refused, as he had promised, to name a particular one. The fund should be broad, holding many companies across many countries, it should have a very low yearly fee, it should be large and established, and it should follow a clear and public index. Mira added one more line of her own, that dividends should be reinvested automatically, and then she began to search.

Mira found a fund that matched every item on her checklist, read its information sheet twice and then pressed the button to place her first order. A moment later the screen announced that the order had been completed, and she realised with a thrill that she now owned a minute piece of thousands of companies in dozens of countries. It was only two hundred dollars, and yet she looked at the confirmation as though it were a diploma.

A month after her first purchase Mira opened the app on her phone, and there in red was a small negative number with a downward arrow beside it. Her account was worth a few dollars less than she had paid in, and although the loss was trivial, she felt her stomach drop as if she had missed a stair. It was her first lesson in how much money can feel like a mood.

For the next week Mira checked her account several times a day, at breakfast, at her desk and under the table at lunch, and her mood rose and fell with the figure on the screen. Her colleague Sana, who sat opposite and noticed everything, remarked that Mira looked like someone watching a very slow football match. Mira laughed, but she suspected that the remark was truer than it was funny.

Mira rang Dev from a bench in the park and confessed that her account had already lost money, and that she did not know whether she had made a mistake. He answered gently that a single month tells you almost nothing about an investment that is meant to last thirty years, because short periods are mostly noise and the signal lives in the long run. If she had expected a straight upward line, he said, she was not the first, and she would not be the last.

Dev made a suggestion that sounded almost too easy: look at the account only now and then, perhaps twice a year, and let the monthly payments carry on regardless. Watching every day would not make the money grow, he said, but it would certainly make the worry grow, and worry is the main thing that makes people do foolish things. That evening Mira moved the app off her front screen, and for good measure she turned off its notifications.

Day by day, Dev explained, the movements of the market are mostly noise, which is why watching them is so exhausting and so unhelpful. In many markets prices rise on only a little more than half of all days, and the long-term gain is built from that slim advantage, accumulated patiently over years of ordinary trading. Mira imagined a tiny ripple on top of an enormous tide, and found that the picture calmed her.

Dev drew a chart that covered many decades of a broad market's history, and the line on it climbed unevenly from the lower left to the upper right, with sharp dips punctuating the whole journey. Mira was struck by how dramatic each fall must have felt at the time and how small it looked from a distance, like a pothole on a long road seen from an aeroplane. Perspective, she realised, was not something that arrives by itself, but something one has to bring along on purpose, like an umbrella.

Falls are not accidents, Dev insisted, but a regular part of what investors pay for the chance of growth. In markets with well-recorded histories, drops of a tenth have happened fairly often and drops of a fifth now and then, and the recoveries have taken anything from a few months to many years. He did not hide the bad news, including the fact that a few markets have taken far longer, and Mira respected him all the more for it.

A price that falls on a screen, Dev said, is not yet a loss that you have suffered, because the loss only becomes real on the day you sell. The genuine dangers lie elsewhere: selling in a panic, paying high costs, putting everything into one place and needing the money at the wrong moment. Mira noticed that all four were mistakes of behaviour and arrangement, which meant that she could avoid them.

On a fresh page of her notebook Mira wrote the heading my plan for bad days and, beneath it, three rules in her neatest handwriting. The first was to keep investing every month, the second was not to sell when prices fell, and the third was to review the plan once a year and at no other time. Writing them down while she was calm, Dev explained, was the whole point, because a frightened person cannot be trusted to invent rules on the spot.

Dev read the three rules aloud, nodded with satisfaction and signed the page with the date, as a witness might sign a contract. A plan is only worth something, he said, if it can be found at the very moment you would prefer to forget it, and so Mira put the notebook into the top drawer of her desk, where it would wait. She had a feeling, which she could not explain, that she would be glad of it one day.

A few months passed, and Mira felt calmer about the small ups and downs, though she still wondered whether she ought to hold some bonds as well. Dev replied that a mixture of shares and bonds tends to smooth the ride, because the two do not always move in the same direction at the same time. He stressed the word tends, since bonds can fall too, and the cushion is never perfect.

Dev compared an investment plan to a sailing boat, and the image stayed with Mira for years. Shares were the sail, he said, giving the speed and the chance of a long journey, while bonds were the keel, which holds the boat steady and keeps it from tipping over when the wind rises. A boat with too little sail goes nowhere, he added, and a boat with no keel will not survive the first storm.

Dev worked through an illustration on the back of an envelope, using invented numbers to make the point clearly. If shares fell by a fifth in a bad year and the bonds merely stood still, a mixture of eighty percent shares and twenty percent bonds would fall by about sixteen percent, which is still painful but easier to bear. In real life the bonds might rise or fall a little, he said, but the principle held: a mixture bends where a single material might break.

Dev mentioned one rule of thumb, which many people have used: hold a percentage of your money in shares equal to one hundred minus your age, so that the share falls as you grow older. For a woman of twenty-eight this gave seventy-two percent, but he insisted that it was only a starting point, a rough sketch rather than a law, and that sensible people choose a number higher or lower than the rule suggests. A rule of thumb, he said, is better than nothing and worse than thinking.

How bold should she be, Mira asked, and Dev replied that two different things decide the answer. The first is her ability to take risk, which depends on her horizon, her job and her emergency fund, and the second is her willingness, which depends on how she feels when the numbers fall. Ability can be calculated, he said, but willingness can only be discovered by honest reflection, and the lower of the two should win.

After several evenings of thought Mira settled on a mixture that leaned heavily towards shares, with a smaller portion in bonds, which she wrote into her notebook as roughly four parts in five and one part in five. She added a note to herself that, if the plan proved too frightening to hold in a real fall, she would adjust it gently in a calm moment and never in a panic. Dev approved, saying that the best mix is the one that a person is able to keep.

Dev told her that some funds package shares and bonds together, and that a few, often called target-date funds, gradually shift towards bonds as a chosen year approaches. They are convenient for people who dislike fiddling, though their fees and their mixtures vary a great deal, so every one of them deserves the same careful reading as any other fund. Mira decided to keep things simple and to use two separate funds, one for shares and one for bonds.

Dev put a small globe into her hands and pointed out that her own country, dear as it was to her, accounted for only a modest share of the world's companies. Many investors hold mostly the shares of their home market, out of familiarity, yet spreading across many countries lowers the risk that one nation's troubles will sink the whole plan. He could not tell her which country would do best in the next decade, he said, and neither could anyone else.

A world fund, Dev explained, holds the shares of companies from dozens of countries, many of which earn their money in different currencies and sell their goods across borders. Changes in exchange rates will add a little extra movement to the value of the fund as seen in Mira's own currency, but he thought that this was a small price to pay for such a wide and sensible spread. She chose a fund that followed a broad index of companies from developed and developing countries alike.

Dev warned her that over time the mix drifts, because if shares rise faster than bonds the shares will come to make up a larger part of the whole than she intended. Once a year, therefore, she should look at the proportions and restore them, either by selling a little of the winner or, more simply, by steering her new monthly payments towards whichever part had fallen behind. This habit, called rebalancing, has a pleasing side effect, for it quietly makes you buy what is cheap.

Many of the companies in her fund paid out a part of their profit to their owners as dividends, Dev explained, and the fund collected all of these payments. Because Mira had chosen to have them reinvested automatically, the money was used to buy yet more units, and those new units would in time earn dividends of their own. It was like a tree that scatters seeds around itself, so that young trees grow up in its shade.

This leads to the idea that Dev called the most powerful in all of investing, which is compounding: the earnings on an investment begin to earn money of their own. It resembles a snowball set rolling down a long slope, which starts as a handful and then picks up more snow with every turn, so that most of its size is gathered near the end. The effect needs one ingredient above all, and that ingredient, he said, is time.

To make the idea concrete Dev showed her a quick rule of thumb, called the rule of seventy-two, which gives a rough answer in the head. Divide seventy-two by the yearly return and you get the approximate number of years needed for money to double, so that six percent doubles money in about twelve years, three percent in about twenty-four and nine percent in about eight. It is an approximation and not a promise, he said, but it showed her at a glance how much a small difference in return can matter.

Dev then showed her an illustration, which was not a forecast, of ten thousand dollars growing at six percent a year for thirty years. It becomes about fifty-seven thousand dollars, but the surprising feature was the shape of the growth, because the final ten years add more than the first twenty years put together. Most of the harvest, he said, arrives late, which is exactly why leaving the money alone is so rewarding.

Next Dev worked out the sum for Mira's own plan, once again as an illustration and not a promise. Two hundred dollars a month for thirty years, at an average of six percent a year, would become about two hundred thousand dollars, of which only seventy-two thousand would be the money that she had actually paid in. The remainder, about a hundred and twenty-eight thousand, was earned by the money itself, and Mira stared at the figure for a long moment.

Dev tried the same two hundred dollars a month with different lengths of time, and the results were a striking lesson in patience. At an average of six percent, twenty years would produce about ninety-two thousand dollars, thirty years about two hundred thousand and forty years nearly three hundred thousand, even though the payments were identical every month. The only difference was how long the money had been allowed to work, and that was entirely a matter of when she began.

Dev reminded her that the six percent in his examples was only an average, and that the real road is never a smooth upward line. Some years would be much better, some much worse, and nobody could say in which order they would arrive, so the actual result could end up higher or lower than any illustration. That uncertainty, he said, was the reason for everything they had discussed about spreading money, keeping costs low and staying calm.

Mr Hale, who owned the small printing company where Mira worked, gave her a modest pay rise, and she read the letter twice with her calculator beside her. Dev's advice was to raise her monthly investment whenever her pay rose, but Mira's second goal was a deposit for a home within seven years, and she decided that the extra money should go to that jar first. She promised herself that once the deposit was ready, her monthly investing would grow too.

Dev fetched his own old statements from a drawer, and Mira saw at once that his monthly payment had risen a little, year by year, in a staircase of small steps. Because each step was so modest, he had hardly noticed any change in his budget, and yet the staircase had carried him to a much larger yearly sum than he had ever planned at the beginning. Small increases, he said, are almost painless when they are spread across the years.

That evening Mira summed up the lesson in her notebook as three ingredients: time, regular payments and reinvested earnings. Of the three, she noticed, only time could never be bought back, since it cannot be added to a plan after the years have passed, whereas the other two are matters of habit and choice. She drew a small snowball at the top of the page, and under it she wrote, in capital letters, start now and then be patient.

At work one morning, Tomas leaned across her desk with his phone held out like a trophy, showing a chart that pointed almost straight up. The price of the company he had bought, he announced, had doubled in a few weeks, and Mira would be mad not to buy some before the chance disappeared. He said it with such warm and generous excitement that it was hard to see it as anything but friendship.

All afternoon Mira felt a strong tug to buy whatever Tomas had bought, and she was surprised by how physical the sensation was, like hunger or itching. Her own steady plan, with its two hundred dollars a month and its quiet index fund, looked painfully dull beside his racing chart, and twice she found her thumb hovering over the app. This was the pull that Dev had warned about, and it felt far stronger in real life than it had sounded in the kitchen.

When she told Dev about her afternoon, he pointed out that people boast loudly about their winning bets and say nothing at all about their losing ones. The result is that a crowd of cheerful stories makes risky choices look far more successful than they are, while the silent majority who lost never appear in the conversation. Mira realised that the loud voice in the office was only one half of a much larger picture.

Dev explained what is called a bubble, in which prices rise because people are excited and then rise further because more people see them rising and join in. At some point the price floats far above anything that the underlying business could justify, and when the mood changes the fall can be swift and brutal. History contains many fashionable assets that lost most of their value in this way, he said, and nobody ever knows beforehand which day the bubble will burst.

Tomas also dabbled in digital coins, which were all the fashion that year, and Dev explained why he treated them with caution. A share represents a business that earns profits and a bond represents a loan that pays interest, but a digital coin pays nothing, so its price depends almost entirely on what the next buyer will pay. Prices of such coins have swung wildly, he said, and for that reason they belonged much nearer to gambling than to investing.

Dev conceded that the itch to gamble is strong in some people, and that if it could not be ignored, it was better to keep a small sum apart. Mira laughed, took a few coins from her purse and dropped them in a jar that she labelled fun, with the rule that it would never be refilled from her investments. The jar sat on the shelf as a joke, but the rule behind it, no more than a few percent and never from the real plan, was perfectly serious.

A month later the price of Tomas's company dropped by half, and he sat at his desk all morning without saying a word. Mira felt no pleasure at all, only a quiet gladness that she had held to her own plan, and she brought him a coffee and a biscuit without making any comment. Dev later told her that this was exactly how such stories usually go, and that it was kindest to treat the matter as nobody's fault.

At a restaurant one evening, Mira's old school friend Bea leaned across the table and whispered that she had heard a secret tip about a small company that was certain to rise. When Mira repeated this to Dev, he said that tips from friends and strangers should be ignored, because a truly valuable tip would never be given away for nothing. Trading on genuine inside information is also illegal in many countries, and a secret told across a table is usually just a rumour in a good coat.

Dev wrote down the warning signs of a scam, because he said that they are astonishingly similar from one swindle to the next. They promise guaranteed or unusually high returns, they push you to hurry, they ask for secrecy or they demand payment in unusual ways, and any one of these is a reason to walk away. Some schemes even pay early investors with the money of later ones, which can look like success until the supply of newcomers runs out.

Beneath her three rules for bad days, Mira added two new ones that came out of all that she had seen that season. The first was that she would never buy anything she could not explain in a couple of plain sentences. The second was that she would not act on a tip from a friend or a stranger, however warmly it was offered, and the page was starting to look like a small constitution.

Some months after she began, Mira received her first full statement from the platform, a document of several pages and many columns. She read it line by line with a pencil in her hand, since Dev had taught her that the charges that matter are often the smallest and the best hidden. Most of the lines were harmless, but the exercise itself felt like a good habit, much as one checks a bill in a restaurant.

Mira added together every cost she could find, namely the yearly fee of the fund and the yearly charge of the platform, and the total came to about a quarter of one percent of her money each year. That was a small fraction of what many people pay, and she was quietly pleased that she had compared the options before choosing instead of simply taking the first one on offer. Dev called the figure her total cost, and told her to know it at all times, like her own address.

There is another small cost, Dev told her, which is the spread, the gap between the price at which you can buy something and the price at which you could sell it at the same moment. For large, popular funds the gap is usually tiny, but for unusual ones it can be wide, and the same goes for the markup that some platforms add when they convert one currency into another. These are not outrageous costs, but they accumulate quietly, and they deserve a place on the list.

Dev warned her about advertisements that shout the word free, because every company has to earn its living from somewhere, and when the customer is not paying openly, the payment is usually hidden in another place. It might come from the spread, from interest on the cash that sits in the account or from selling more complicated products to people who had come only for something simple. Mira began to ask of every service the question that Dev always asked, which was how it was paid.

Mira began to wonder whether she ought to talk to a professional adviser, in case she had overlooked something important in all her careful reading. Dev said that the right adviser can be very helpful, but that the title is not protected in every country, so she should choose a regulated one and look the person up on the public register before booking an appointment. Neither he nor she, he added, should be treated as the last word on her particular circumstances.

The way an adviser is paid, Dev emphasised, shapes the advice more than most people realise. Some charge a flat or hourly fee, some take a percentage of your money every year, and some earn commission from the products they recommend, which can quietly tempt them towards the expensive choice. A good question for any adviser, he said, was simply: how will you earn money if I do what you suggest?

Mira booked a single hour with Ms Lindqvist, a regulated adviser who charged a flat fee and took no commission from anyone, and she arrived with her notebook and a list of questions. She began by asking how the adviser earned her living, and Ms Lindqvist smiled with evident approval and laid out her fees in a single plain sentence. It was a small, pleasant meeting in a plain room, and nobody tried to sell her anything.

Ms Lindqvist read through Mira's notebook with unhurried attention and then said that the plan was sound, simple and well suited to its purpose. She suggested a few small improvements concerning the tax rules of Mira's country and the paperwork she should keep, and she added candidly that many people with plans like hers do not need an adviser every year. Mira left feeling steadier than before, and not at all poorer for the flat fee.

Mira found an old shoebox for the paper documents and made a matching folder on her computer, and into these she put her statements, her order confirmations, a simple spreadsheet of her monthly purchases and anything that related to tax. Dev had told her that a simple and orderly record is worth far more than it costs, both for the tax authorities and for her own peace of mind, and she found it was true. It took ten minutes each quarter, it cost nothing at all, and it let her sleep a little better at night.

Dev reminded her that in many countries dividends and gains may be taxed, sometimes at different rates and sometimes not at all inside certain accounts. The rules vary so widely that no general book could safely tell her what to do, so Mira wrote the relevant dates on her calendar and read the official guidance for her country. She promised herself that she would ask a tax professional about anything she did not fully understand, since the alternative was an unpleasant surprise.

Dev told Mira that the number on a statement is only half of the story, because what truly matters is how much the money can buy. For that reason investors look at returns after inflation, which is called the real return, since a gain that merely matches rising prices leaves you no better off than before. It was the same lesson as the two lines on the napkin at the beginning, and Mira smiled to see how far she had travelled since then.

Dev gave her an example with round numbers, stressing as usual that they were illustrations. If an investment grew by six percent in a year while prices rose by two percent, the real gain was roughly four percent. Cash earning only one percent, by contrast, would lose about one percent of its buying power each year, which is why doing nothing was never quite as safe as it looked.

Dev then applied the idea to Mira's own long plan, with an honesty that she appreciated. If prices rose by two percent a year for thirty years they would end up about eighty percent higher. The two hundred thousand dollars of his earlier illustration would then buy roughly what one hundred and ten thousand buys today, a still useful sum whose true size she was better off knowing now.

Dev drew a distinction that Mira wrote in capital letters: time in the market is what builds wealth, whereas timing the market is a game that very few can win. Anyone who tries to dodge the falls must make two correct decisions, when to leave and when to return, and the second is usually harder than the first because the recovery tends to start while the news is still bad. Staying put, he said, only requires the courage to do nothing, and that courage is rarer than any cleverness.

As a game, Mira and her colleagues stuck notes on the office calendar each Friday, predicting whether the market would rise or fall in the following week. At the end of the month nobody had done noticeably better than a coin toss, and even Tomas, who had boasted loudly about his instincts, was forced to laugh at the result. It was a harmless experiment, but it left everyone slightly humbler, which is the beginning of sound investing.

Dev mentioned that studies of several large markets have found a curious pattern: the best days often arrive close to the worst days, in the same turbulent stretches. An investor who jumps out during a fall may therefore miss the handful of enormous days on which much of the long-term gain is made, and the missed days can cost a surprising amount over the decades. Nobody rings a bell, he said, to say that the bottom has been reached.

Mira began to notice that the financial headlines are written to be urgent, that they always find a reason for each day's movement and that they never say that nothing important has happened. She decided to read the news only once a week, as she might look at the weather before a trip, and she resolved that her plan would not alter with any headline. The quiet, she found, did not make her ignorant, only more peaceful, and it left her more time for her real life.

After a full year Mira sat down with a cup of tea and opened her account for the first time in months, curious about what she would find. She had paid in two thousand four hundred dollars, and the account was worth a little more than that, which was no marvel, but proved that nothing terrible had happened while she was not looking. She felt the quiet satisfaction of someone who has kept a promise to herself.

At Sunday lunch in Dev's garden, his wife Anita asked how Mira's investing was going, and their young son Rohan, who had been listening with a sausage in his hand, asked what an index fund was. Mira thought for a moment and told him that it was a very big basket with a tiny bit of lots of companies in it, so that if one went wrong the rest could carry on. Rohan nodded, satisfied, and Mira realised that if a six-year-old could follow the idea, it was probably a sound one.

By the thirteenth month prices had risen steadily for a long time, the headlines were cheerful and Mira found it easy to forget that the market ever fell. Dev, who had seen several such periods, warned her gently that calm seas do not last for ever and that this was exactly the right moment to remember her rules, while her mind was quiet. That night she took the notebook out of the drawer, read her three rules slowly and put it back, without quite knowing why.

In her fourteenth month of investing, Mira walked to work in a steady drizzle and passed a shop window where a bank of screens flashed red headlines. The market had fallen sharply overnight, and the voices of the news presenters had the grave and hurried tone that people use when they believe something dreadful is under way. She stopped under her umbrella and watched for a full minute, feeling the rain on her sleeves and a cold knot growing in her stomach.

At the printing company that morning no one was printing anything, because the whole staff had gathered around a computer screen to watch the numbers fall. Tomas was pale and silent, Mr Hale walked up and down with his hands behind his back, and somebody near the kettle announced that this was the end of everything. Mira stood at the edge of the little crowd and noticed that fear spreads through a room as easily as a yawn.

The fall did not stop in a single day, but continued in jolts over the following weeks, with a brief recovery here and a fresh drop there, until the market had lost roughly a fifth of its value. Because Mira held some bonds as well as shares, her own account fell by somewhat less, which was just what Dev had said would happen, though the figure on her screen still felt like a punch. Fourteen months of patient payments seemed to be shrinking before her eyes, and the future looked suddenly smaller too.

That week Mira slept badly, waking at three in the morning to reach for her phone and check the number, and each time she looked she felt slightly sick. She had promised herself that she would look only now and then, and the broken promise made her feel doubly foolish, as if she had failed a test that she had set herself. In the dark, with nobody to contradict it, every argument for selling sounded perfectly reasonable and almost wise.

A calm and sensible voice began to speak in Mira's head, saying that she should sell now, save what remained and buy back later when everything looked safe again. It sounded so logical that she nearly obeyed, but then she remembered Dev's warning that safe never announces itself, and that by the time the news becomes cheerful the prices have usually risen already. The voice, she realised, was not wisdom but fear dressed up in a suit.

Tomas announced to the whole office that he had sold everything he owned, with the air of a man who has narrowly escaped a flood. He would buy again, he said, as soon as the market was safe, and Mira, who had been listening quietly, wondered how he planned to recognise that day when it came. Nobody, she suspected, would send him a letter to announce that the danger had passed, and the recovery would probably begin without him.

One evening, after another poor night and a gloomy day, Mira found her finger hovering above the sell button on her phone screen, trembling very slightly. She understood, with a strange clarity, that this was exactly the moment for which she had written her plan, a moment when she could not trust her own mood or the voice in her head. She turned the phone face down on the table and stepped away from it.

Mira opened the top drawer of her desk, took out the plain notebook and found the page that Dev had signed months earlier. She read the three rules aloud in the quiet room, slowly, as though they had been written by a wiser friend: keep investing every month, do not sell in a fall, and review the plan only once a year. It was strange to hear her own calm voice from the past, telling her what to do.

Under the signed rules Mira wrote one more line, a cooling-off rule of her own devising: before making any decision about her investments in a fall, she would wait three whole days. She copied it on a card and taped it to the bathroom mirror, where she would be sure to read it before she had time to feel brave or frightened. Most decisions made in a panic, she reflected, look different once the pulse has slowed.

Dev, who had been watching the news with a very different feeling from Mira's, knew exactly how she must be suffering, and on a wet Sunday morning he got into his car and drove to her house. On the passenger seat beside him lay an old and worn notebook with a cracked spine, which he had not shown to anyone for years, and he had decided that the time had come. The windscreen wipers beat steadily against the rain, and he rehearsed again and again what he would say when she opened the door.

Dev arrived at Mira's door with rain dripping from his shoulders and a worn notebook tucked under his arm, and he apologised for turning up without warning. Mira, who had never been so pleased to see anyone, made strong tea and cleared a space at the kitchen table, and for a moment neither of them spoke. The kettle's steady hiss was the most comforting sound she had heard all month.

Mira laid her notebook open at the signed page, and Dev read it with a smile that he did not trouble to hide. Then he opened his own, whose pages were yellow and soft at the corners, and she saw that its first plan, written ten years earlier, looked remarkably like her own. It was clear that the cousins shared a habit as well as a name, and that the habit had been learned the hard way.

Then Dev told her the story that he had promised on the first Sunday. Ten years earlier, two years after he had started investing, the market had fallen by about a third over a few anxious months. He had watched his account shrink until he lost his nerve and sold everything in a single afternoon, and he could still remember the cold relief of pressing the button and how quickly it had turned sour.

Within weeks of his sale the market touched its lowest point and began to climb, although the news stayed gloomy for months, and Dev, who was waiting for a clear sign that it was safe, did nothing at all. When he finally bought again, the prices were far higher than the ones at which he had sold, and he calculated that his panic had cost him a few thousand dollars and more than two years of progress. It was a very expensive lesson, and he had paid for it in cash and in pride.

Dev explained, to comfort her, that psychologists have repeatedly found that a loss tends to hurt roughly twice as much as an equal gain gives pleasure, a tendency known as loss aversion. This lopsided feeling is one of the main reasons that investors sell in a fall and avoid buying when prices are low, and it showed that Mira's distress was no sign of weakness. It was simply how human beings are made, and the remedy was to know it and to plan accordingly.

In his old notebook one line had been underlined three times in a hand that was clearly angry: never decide in a storm. The paper loss, Dev said, had become a real loss on the day he sold, and he had sold at the bottom exactly what he should have been buying. Mira copied the line onto the page beneath her own four rules and underlined it twice, as if the pencil could make it permanent.

After that costly mistake Dev wrote himself a plan, made his payments automatic and decided to check his account only twice a year. When the market fell again a few years later, he did absolutely nothing, which felt dull and slightly unreal, and he told Mira that it was the best investment decision of his life. Doing nothing, he explained, is an underrated skill, and like most skills it improves with practice.

Dev then showed her a simple piece of arithmetic that she found, rather to her own surprise, oddly cheering. When the price of a unit falls by a fifth, her monthly two hundred dollars buys about a quarter more units than it did before, and those extra units will benefit fully if and when prices recover. The fall that hurt her account was therefore also putting her future payments on sale, though he was careful to say that nobody could know how long the sale would last.

Mira made up her mind in the quiet of the kitchen: her next payment would leave her bank account on its usual date, exactly as the plan said, and she would not touch the settings. Then she asked Dev to stay for dinner, and she was surprised to discover, for the first time in weeks, that she was hungry. They cooked pasta together, burned the garlic and laughed about it, and the conversation drifted gently far from money.

Before she went to bed that night Mira opened her notebook and wrote a dated line beneath the rest, in the steady handwriting of someone who had slept badly for weeks and was about to sleep well. The market fell by about a fifth this month, she wrote, I was afraid, and I kept going. It was a small sentence, but she read it twice with a feeling very close to pride.

On the usual morning the next payment left Mira's bank account without any help from her, and the platform used it to buy units at the lower prices of the day. She had not touched a single setting, and she had the curious feeling of having done something brave without lifting a finger. That, she realised, was precisely what automatic payments are for: they lend courage to the days when courage is in short supply.

A few weeks later the prices stopped falling and began, almost imperceptibly, to creep upwards, although the headlines remained as gloomy as ever. Nobody rang a bell at the bottom, and Mira learned only long afterwards, by looking at the chart, that the worst day had already passed. Had she sold in the autumn, as the voice in her head had urged, she would have missed the whole of the recovery.

Tomas, meanwhile, stayed in cash and waited for a clear sign that all was well, and each month, as the prices rose a little higher, he told Mira with a weary smile that it was too late now. Mira felt a sympathetic pang, because she understood that his difficulty was not stupidity but fear, and she knew how easily it could have been hers. She said nothing smug and nothing wise, and merely asked whether he would like to have lunch with her in the park.

Months passed, and Mira's life filled up with ordinary pleasures: morning runs in the park, evenings of cooking for friends and busy days at the printing company. Her plan went on working in the background without needing her attention, as a good heating system keeps a house warm without anyone thinking about it, and her thoughts were free for other things. The most successful part of investing, she was learning, is how little of one's life it needs to occupy.

When she looked at her mix during a calm moment, Mira saw that it had drifted, since shares had fallen further than bonds and now made up a smaller part of the whole than she had planned. Instead of selling anything she simply steered her new monthly payments towards the shares until the balance was restored, which meant that she was buying the cheaper part in the very season when it was cheap. Rebalancing, she noticed, makes a virtue of discomfort, because it asks you to favour whatever has recently disappointed you.

Mira chose one fixed day each year for her review, the first Sunday after her birthday, and drew up a short checklist to follow on that day and no other. It asked whether her emergency fund was still enough, whether her mix was still right, whether her costs had crept up, whether her payments were still running and whether anything in her life had changed. Conspicuously, and deliberately, it did not ask how much money she had made or lost, nor what the news had been saying.

At her first yearly review Mira worked through every item on the list with a pencil and found, a little to her own surprise, that nothing needed to change. She told Dev proudly that the whole process had taken forty minutes, and he replied that a review which changes nothing is not wasted but a success. A good plan, he explained, is built to be left alone for most of the time, and Mira filed that sentence in the part of her mind where she kept her best lessons.

Some two years after the great fall, the market finally climbed back to the high point that it had reached before, and a quiet graph rose behind Mira as she worked at her desk. Her account was now worth more than all she had paid into it, and she looked at the figure with relief and a warm sense of vindication. The long wait, which had once seemed unbearable, had passed as quietly as a winter that nobody notices ending.

Dev pointed out that Mira's account had recovered somewhat sooner than the market itself, and he explained the reason with evident delight. Because she had gone on buying through the fall, a good number of her units had been bought at low prices, and these units had gained the most when the recovery came. It was a small reward for her steadiness, though he reminded her that the order of good and bad years is never guaranteed to be so kind.

In her notebook Mira wrote down what the fall had taught her, and she took her time over the words. She had not been brave in the storm, she admitted, but she had a plan, and a plan is a kind of courage that you lend yourself in advance, to be repaid when the day of fear arrives. She read the sentence aloud and thought that it was the best she had ever written.

A good plan, Dev told her, should be left strictly alone when the news changes, but reviewed carefully when your life changes. A new job, a new home, a child, an illness or a sudden windfall can each be a sound reason to adjust the plan, whereas a frightening headline never is. It was a distinction that she found useful far beyond money, and she wrote it on the first page of her notebook.

In her third year of investing, Mira received a letter from her landlord informing her that the flat was being sold and that she would need to leave within two months. It was an unwelcome shock, particularly because moving always costs more than anyone expects, with deposits, a van, new furniture and a dozen small bills. She read the letter at the kitchen table and then, rather to her own surprise, felt calm.

The move cost her a good deal, but it was exactly the sort of event for which Mira had set up her jars, and she paid for it from the jar marked soon. She did not touch her emergency fund, which stayed whole for real emergencies, and she did not sell a single unit of her long-term investments, which could carry on growing in the background. Seldom had a plan seemed so neatly vindicated, and she felt a quiet gratitude towards the person who had written it, which was herself.

Dev and Anita told Mira, with shining eyes, that they were expecting a second baby, and Dev described with a bookkeeper's care how he was already adjusting the family's plan. He would enlarge the emergency fund, check the insurance cover for the family, and think about how to save for the child's future needs, while the long-term investing carried on exactly as before. A growing family, he said, is an excellent reason to review a plan and a very poor reason to abandon one.

Mira's dream of a home of her own was getting nearer, and Dev reminded her of the rule that she had written in the first month: money needed within about five years does not belong in shares. A fall in the market just before she wished to buy could shrink the deposit at the worst possible moment, and the small extra growth that shares might offer did not justify such a danger. She kept the deposit in safe savings, where it was dull and dependable, and she did not mind.

One morning Mr Hale gathered the staff and announced that the printing company would begin a workplace pension scheme, and he distributed a letter that explained how it worked. At home that evening Mira read the letter twice at her kitchen table and discovered that her employer would add money to her pension whenever she paid in, up to a certain limit. She was delighted that she had learned enough over the past two years to ask the right questions without feeling foolish.

The scheme, as Dev explained when she showed him the letter, worked in a refreshingly simple way. If Mira paid in three percent of her pay, her employer would add a further three percent, so that she doubled that part of her saving on the very first day, which amounted to a kind of extra pay. In many countries, he said, taking an employer's match, if one is offered, is one of the few things in finance that is close to free, though the rules differ and she should read them carefully.

Mira turned to the pension's information pack and asked the same two questions that she had learned to ask about every fund, namely what was inside it and what it cost. The default fund was quite sensible, a broad mixture that moved gradually towards safer holdings as she grew older, but she found another option that was broader still and charged a lower yearly fee. She noted both choices in her notebook and made her selection with the calm confidence of someone who had done it before.

Dev reminded her that in many countries the government also pays a state pension, though the amount and the age at which it begins differ from place to place, and may well change in the decades ahead. Mira found the official forecast for her own country, studied it carefully and concluded that it would be helpful but probably not sufficient on its own, which made her private saving feel more valuable. It was another case in which a little reading brought a great deal of clarity.

On a clean page Mira drew her entire financial life as four jars, which she labelled emergency, soon, long-term investing and pension, and she gave each of them a different job and a different amount of risk. Beneath the drawing she wrote a rule for the times when life changes: change the plan on purpose and on paper, and never in a hurry. Dev studied the page for some time and then said that it was the clearest financial plan that he had ever seen on a single sheet.

During another small dip in the market, when the office buzzed with complaints, Mira carried on with her work in a cheerful and untroubled way. Her colleague Sana, a young woman who had joined the printing company only that year, noticed the difference and asked quietly how Mira had ever learned to invest. Mira realised that she had become, without any plan to do so, the person at work whom others asked about money.

At lunch in a nearby cafe Mira took a paper napkin and drew a plan in four boxes, exactly as Dev had once drawn two lines for her. The boxes read emergency savings, low costs, regular payments and patience, and Sana studied them with wide eyes as though they were a map to buried treasure. It occurred to Mira that the whole of her education had been compressed into a few words on a scrap of paper.

Sana asked, with the honest suspicion of a beginner, whether investing was not simply gambling with a more respectable name. Mira borrowed a sugar packet, a coin and a button from her bag and lined them up on the cafe table, repeating the lesson that Dev had given her years before about saving, investing and speculating. Teaching it aloud, she noticed with a small thrill, made her understand the ideas better than she ever had in the kitchen.

Mira told Sana to start where she herself had started, with an emergency fund and the clearing of any costly debt, long before a single dollar went into the market. After that she must read every cost, check that any platform was regulated and never trust anybody who promised a result, because honest people in this business do not make promises. Sana wrote it all in her phone, and Mira gave her a spare notebook with a pen clipped to the cover.

Mira had come to see that the most valuable advice she had received was also the most boring, and she began to suspect that this was not an accident. A simple plan, with low costs, wide spreading and regular payments, is easy to understand and cheap to keep, and it can be followed for decades by a person who is tired, busy and sometimes frightened. Anything complicated gives the mind many more chances to wander off, to be tempted and to make expensive mistakes.

Looking back over the years, Mira saw that her best decisions had been the things that she had not done. She had not sold in the fall, she had not chased a hot tip, she had not paid high fees and she had not watched the screen every day. Each of those refusals had saved her more than any clever move could have earned, and the plan, she reflected, was mostly a list of temptations resisted.

Five years after her first payment, Mira had paid in twelve thousand dollars, and her account was worth a little more than that, having been pushed and pulled by both good years and bad ones along the way. It was not a fortune, and it was not meant to be, but it was real, it was growing and the habit behind it was now as natural as brushing her teeth. Dev, sitting beside her with his tea, said that this was exactly how it should look after five patient years.

Best of all, Mira no longer felt that investing was a locked room whose key belonged to other people, and she thought of the evening when she had first rung Dev with a head full of fear. She knew, too, that the next five years might be kinder or harsher than the last five, because no one can promise otherwise, and she felt ready for either. What she possessed now was not a prediction but a plan, and a plan, she had learned, is worth more.

They walked together through the park at sunset, the old notebook under Mira's arm, and Dev asked what she would say to herself on the evening that she turned twenty-eight and rang him for help. Mira thought for a long moment, watching the light slide through the trees, and said that she would tell herself to begin, to keep it simple and to be gentle with herself on the bad days. Dev laughed, because that was almost exactly what he would have said, and he added that it was also what he told himself.

The plan, in the end, was short enough to fit on a napkin: build your savings first, invest regularly in broad, low-cost funds, spread your money widely and stay calm when prices fall. Nobody can promise results, and every investment carries some risk of loss, so the sensible course is to begin small, learn as you go and be patient with the years.
